Q: Github resolving conflicts always merges base branch to my current branch A:

We faced a similar issue. As a workaround, whenever there are conflicts in the current PR (for example, from feature1 to qa), we create a new PR with qa as the source branch and feature1 as the base branch. After resolving the conflicts and completing the merge, the updated feature1 branch can then be merged cleanly into qa.

Q: Question about retry logic in usb-skeleton.c skel_read() A:

The code presented in the question doesn't appear to be from Linus's current usb-skeleton.c, nor does it look anywhere near complete. I suspect that you've cut down the original code to extract what you take to be the essentials. The result of such an effort is not something we can analyze in detail, because context is important, plus there is a high risk of such an editing process removing details essential for understanding the points you're asking about.

Speaking in general, however, the code presented seems stitched together from pieces consistent with what I would expect for the kernel's behavior on servicing a read() request:

  1. Successfully transfer 0 bytes if that's what was requested. Otherwise,

  2. If the file is in non-blocking mode, no bytes can be transferred without blocking, and EOF has not yet been detected, then fail with EAGAIN. Otherwise,

  3. Block if necessary until at least one byte can be transferred or EOF is detected, then successfully transfer the lesser of the number of bytes requested and the number bytes available without (further) blocking.

Note in particular that read() does not guarantee that the full number of bytes requested will in fact be transferred, and that's not only to accommodate reaching end of file. Except for files in non-blocking mode, however, read() does guarantee to either indicate EOF or transfer at least one byte on a request for more than zero bytes.

You note:

On entry : Waits for ongoing_read (or returns -EAGAIN if O_NONBLOCK)

Yes, this is essential.

When data < count : Submits URB but returns immediately without waiting

Starting a new read request appears to be an optimization. The driver has already read all the data it needs to or intends to provide to the user on this read() call, but because it's a short read, the driver guesses that an additional read() of the same device will soon be requested. It gets started on that right away to improve overall throughput.

  1. Is the current behavior intentional, or is it simplified for educational purposes?

The general thrust of the code presented is consistent with my expectations, and in particular, I take the difference you call out to be intentional, to the extent that it faithfully reflects the real code. In fact, the corresponding original code contains a comment that specifically speaks to this:

          /*
           * if we are asked for more than we have,
           * we start IO but don't wait
           */
          if (available < count)
                  skel_do_read_io(dev, count - chunk);

So yes, it is intentional that the driver initiates a new read, but returns without waiting for it to complete.

The code presented in the question does seem to have been trimmed down by someone, but I cannot confidently judge the intentions of those edits. They do not appear to mislead with respect to this particular detail of the driver's behavior.

  1. Am I missing any negative side effects of adding goto retry?

Yes. It would make the driver less responsive. I/O is among the slowest things a computer does. Sometimes the userspace code performing the read() needs all the data requested before it can proceed, but other times it can do useful work while additional data are being transferred. Drivers are typically implemented to support the latter case well, because only the userspace code knows which applies, and that code can easily perform additional read() requests before proceeding if it chooses.

Note also that there might not actually be any more bytes to transfer, but if that's not already being indicated then the client will need to issue another read() to discover it anyway.

  1. Is there a USB Bulk transfer characteristic that requires enforcing Short Reads?

Requires, no. But any time a full read would require more blocking than a short read would, the short read is the right thing to do (from the kernel's perspective).

Q: How to parse a xml feed using feed parser python? A:

Try the following basic code, which works fine for me and gave me 10 items in the feed when I ran it.

  1. Install feedparser from pip
pip install feedparser
  1. Usage
import urllib2
import feedparser

url = "https://news.google.com/news?q=fashion&output=rss"
response = urllib2.urlopen(url).read()

print response

d = feedparser.parse(response)
print len(d.entries)
for item in d.entries:
    print "------"
    print item.title
    if 'subtitle' in item:
        print item.subtitle
    print item.link
    print item.description
    print item.published
    print item.id
    print item.updated
    if 'content' in item:
        print item.content

Or, paste the FULL code you're running, and I'll take a look.

Q: Combine JSON to YAML list A:

You could use ireduce to successively build up the result object:

yq ea -oy '
  {filename: .} as $doc ireduce ({}; . + $doc) | {"mystuff": .}
' "${files[@]}"

This would prints something along the lines of

mystuff:
  file1.json:
    first: content
  file2.json:
    second: content

Tested with mikefarah/yq version v4.47.1

Q: KeyVaultCryptoProvider.Create method is failing when we upgrade to .net core 8.0 A:

NET 8 because KeyVaultCryptoProvider is part of the legacy Azure Key Vault SDK that depends on deprecated authentication and crypto APIs (ADAL + older .NET crypto plumbing), which are no longer supported or compatible in .NET 8.

Q: What is logging error when running pip install and how to fix it? A:

My best guess would be to unistall python 3.7 on your machine and try again. It's seem to be trying to print the end of the log message with an uncompatible lib.
